title: Computability, Unsolvability, Randomness
byline: Stephen G. Simpson · Penn State lecture notes (2007), draft of February 2009
note: Lecture notes taken during a one-semester course; homework sets, comments and solutions are interleaved with the sections and are not broken down separately. Summaries are in our own words; the text stays in the PDF.
summary: An undergraduate course in recursion theory that ends at algorithmic randomness. It builds computability from register machines and primitive recursion, defines partial recursive functions with Gödel numbering, the enumeration and parametrization theorems, and proves the halting problem and other natural problems unsolvable, including word problems in group theory and Hilbert’s tenth problem. It then classifies unsolvable problems by the arithmetical hierarchy and by Turing degrees with oracles and the jump. The last third covers Kolmogorov complexity, effectively open and closed sets in Cantor space, Martin-Löf randomness and its characterization by initial-segment complexity, and advanced results such as the low basis theorem and the Kučera–Gács theorem.
